I'm working through the derivation of grah with the yaṅ intensive suffix: samprasāraṇa applies by the grahi-jyā rule since yaṅ is ṅit, giving gṛh, then reduplication and the ṛkāra-to-rī change yield jarīgṛhya.

When ṇic is added, the yā of the yaṅ-anta is dropped before the ārdhadhātuka suffix per 6.4.49. The question is whether this triggers guṇa of the upadhā via 7.3.86 — but since ṇic itself is the cause of that ya-lopa, rule 1.1.4 (na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke) blocks the guṇa from applying, so the correct form stays jarīgṛhi rather than jarīgarhi.

I'm recalling Kāśikā examples like "lolūyaḥ", "popūyaḥ", "marīmṛjaḥ" where yaṅ-luk combined with ac doesn't trigger guṇa, trying to pin down the exact derivations.

With ṇic after yaṅ, I get bebhidya + ṇic undergoing ya-lopa, then checking whether laghūpadha guṇa is blocked by the prohibition—since the yalopa is caused by the ārdhadhātuka ṇic itself, I conclude jarīgṭhi is correct. Now I'm working through what happens when san is added to jarīgṛhi, specifically whether iṭ augment applies.

Since the ṇijanta is aneka-ac, san takes seṭ, giving guṇa and yielding jarīgṛhayiṣa before further suffixing. The tricky part is whether san's reduplication rule applies again on top of the already-reduplicated yaṅ stem, and I'm trying to recall analogous forms like bobhūyiṣati to see if double reduplication actually occurs in yaṅ+san combinations.

Trying to work out whether "jarīgṛhi+san" would re-reduplicate to something like "jajarīgṛhayiṣati" — that seems off, so I'm leaning toward no extra reduplication, though I'm not fully certain and want to check the Pāṇinian justification for how 6.1.9 applies to an already-reduplicated dhātu.

Right, 6.1.8 "liṭi dhātor anabhyāsasya" confirms the anuvṛtti of "anabhyāsasya" into 6.1.9, meaning reduplication only applies to a dhātu that doesn't already have an abhyāsa — so jarīgṛhi, already reduplicated, skips further reduplication, giving jarīgṛhayiṣa. Adding the upasargas abhi+sam gives either abhisañjarīgṛhayiṣati or abhisaṃjarīgṛhayiṣati, both valid depending on whether the nasal assimilates to ñ.
